Article Title: Prasidh Krishna likely to be out of action for three weeks; touch and go for New Zealand ODIs
Article Text:
India's Prasidh Krishna (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India pacer Prasidh Krishna is set to be out of action for at least three weeks and could be touch and go for the five-match ODI series against New Zealand, beginning November 4.Prasidh sustained a left hamstring injury during the second ODI against the West Indies in Guwahati and subsequently missed the third match of the series in New Chandigarh. He bowled just five overs in the Guwahati ODI before leaving the field in the 31st over of the West Indies innings. He picked up one wicket in the match and has three wickets from the two ODIs he has played in the series.The 30-year-old is also doubtful for the opening round of the Ranji Trophy, which begins on October 11. Karnataka will open their campaign against Andhra Pradesh in Vijayawada.It is learnt that Prasidh has checked into the BCCI's Centre of Excellence (CoE) in his hometown Bengaluru. He is expected to regain full fitness in around three weeks and could start bowling at full intensity in four weeks.His recovery timeline could make his availability for the New Zealand series a tricky proposition. Even if he returns to bowling by then, there is no guarantee that he will be ready to play from the start of the series.India could also be forced to manage their fast bowlers carefully, with Test-bound players expected to miss the last two ODIs against New Zealand.India captain Shubman Gill had admitted after the defeat in New Chandigarh that the absence of players due to injuries and scheduling issues had been frustrating.“I would say it’s been unfortunate, you know, with the injuries and with the scheduling with the other matches being around. It’s been a little bit unfortunate that we have not been able to play the bowling lineup that we would like to,” Gill told reporters.Gill is hopeful of having a full-strength squad available for the New Zealand ODIs, as India look to settle on their preferred combination ahead of the 2027 ODI World Cup.“I honestly think there is not that much time to experiment. The combination that we want to play, hopefully, we get all the players available from the next series. The combination that we would like to play in the World Cup, we want to start playing with that combination,” he said.Prasidh's fitness is therefore a significant concern for India. He is expected to be an important part of the team's plans for the New Zealand tour and the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe. His injury adds to India's growing list of concerns ahead of an important phase in their preparations.
Article Summary: India pacer Prasidh Krishna is set to be out of action for at least three weeks. Krishna sustained a left hamstring injury during the second ODI against the West Indies in Guwahati. The 30-year-old is also doubtful for the opening round of the Ranji Trophy.

Article Title: 'Taking medicines and playing every day': How Koneru Humpy battled diarrhoea to win two medals at Chess Olympiad | Exclusive
Article Text:

Playing through it

Humpy's best Olympiad personally, a difficult one for the team

What's next?

NEW DELHI: What does playing for India actually mean for an athlete? At what point does physical pain become too much? When does the body simply say enough? The Indian teams at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, found themselves answering that question in their own way.Both the open and women’s teams had players battling illness during the tournament, yet both still walked away with medals - silver for the open team and bronze for the women. Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa, playing Board 1 for the open team, had already told TimesofIndia.com how he shook off a rare bout of cold and fever to help India secure team silver while also claiming an individual bronze.For Koneru Humpy, the ordeal was even tougher. The Board 1 player was under the weather for almost the entirety of the Olympiad, but still finished with 7/10 and two bronze medals, one for the team and another individually.Speaking to this website after her double medal at the 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad, Humpy revealed that she had barely had any time to recover before illness struck."It was quite tiring for me because I also played the Global Chess League (GCL) before the Olympiad and, before GCL, I played the US Cairns Cup and one WR event in France," she said. "So I was at home just for four or five days in between, and in those days, I was also attending the online camp.The last two months have been quite a hectic schedule for me."The toll showed up almost as soon as the only rest day (after Round 6) in the schedule had passed."After the rest day, I completely fell sick. I was having diarrhoea, stomach ache, then I was taking medicines. So it was really tough for me," she revealed.What kept her at the board through it wasn't stubbornness so much as a sense of duty to the team. "Probably if it was not representing India, if it was a private team event, I would have taken a rest and asked the other player to play," she added. "But I felt like my presence was very important to hold on the top board, and since Vaishali was also not in good shape, I never had the thought of taking a rest. Somehow, I was just taking medicine and going and playing every day. "That struggle even made it onto camera, with a video from the event capturing the Indian chess legend taking her medication."Oh, yes," she recalled. "I could not get this antibiotic. I was having some other medicines. So somehow we managed to get it from one of our Indian friends. They just handed it to me before the game, so that's how it came in the video."Explaining what could have contributed to her condition, the 39-year-old added, "Probably since I've been eating food from outside for so many months, it kind of affected me. After starting this antibiotic, I think it was much better when I was playing the last round."I think it's very obvious when you have this outside food too much, because you can't avoid it when you travel for tournaments. You have to eat in different places. Of course, as a teenager, you'll be able to resist more. Probably when you age further, you'll have more and more issues."It was against that backdrop that Humpy produced one of the sharpest results of her campaign, a 25-move win over Georgia’s Nana Dzagnidze in the final round, despite everything her body had been through, to secure individual bronze."In fact, I was surprised by her opening choice. I didn't expect it at all," she said with a laugh. "I played it over the board, and she made quite a big mistake, probably she just miscalculated and allowed this sacrifice. It was not working in the previous move, but when I played rook to h3 (18.Rh3), that was the intention. She had to just play king to h8 and escape from this mating net."She missed a tactical resource in between that would have let her get away, so I think I managed to calculate well and accurately to finish off the game."Humpy, playing on the toughest board available, expected a far tougher fight as she acknowledged, "I expected an even tougher fight in the final round and, looking at her opening choice, I felt like she's well prepared and just wanted to hold the top board while the rest of the team fought it out. It seems that was their strategy, from what I saw of her opening."The win, though, didn't come with much breathing room for India as a team."As soon as I won the game, Divya blundered, allowing a big tactic for her opponent. It kind of didn't give any big advantage for us because of her loss. But again, we got lucky with Savitha on the fourth board, where we were completely losing and then she managed to hold it," she added.Now that the dust has settled, Humpy rates this campaign as the strongest of her career on a personal level, even with the team falling short of a repeat gold."When we started for the Olympiad, the expectations were high because of the previous gold," she said. "But practically, it's not easy to retain the title as a team. So I just wanted to take this tournament like any other classical event and give my best."The Grandmaster, India's No. 1 in the women's section, continued, "If I compare all my Olympiads, probably this is the best one, because whenever I've played the Olympiad before, I've lost some rating. This is the first time I've gained rating and also won an individual medal in the tournament, and I stayed unbeaten on the top board. I think I played pretty decent; I've been very stable, not taking too many risks, and when there was a need for a win, I was able to deliver it in the final round. "As a team, though, she doesn't mince words. "I think it was a big failure, because we also had Vaishali in bad shape. She lost two important, crucial matches, against Poland and Kazakhstan, and that actually affected the team result. We still had a chance against China. I can't say we were unlucky, because we've been lucky many times on the fourth board," Humpy elaborated."We were losing in several games, probably four or five, but it just turned around completely, unexpectedly. So I'd say our crucial drawback was not having Vaishali in shape. Though we were very strong on paper, in practicality it was a bit handicapped without her; it was basically me and Divya as the main players, with Vantika and Savitha holding the third and fourth boards."Asked directly whether the health scares or Vaishali's form had been the bigger obstacle, she pointed past both to the sheer physical load of the schedule itself."For me personally, it was more challenging to maintain the energy to play all the games, because I only took a break in round two. From then onwards, I played all nine remaining games, 10 out of 11 in total. It was also a difficult decision for the coaches, whom to place and whom to rest," she recalled. "It used to take up a lot of time every day, but that call was completely theirs. I never interfered in those decisions, despite being a senior member. "There's no long break built in just yet."I have the European Club Cup starting from October 17th, so I'll play that," she said. "So far, that's all I've confirmed. After that, I'll probably have some break in November."As for the next Olympiad cycle, two years out, Humpy isn't ready to look that far ahead.READ ALSO: ‘Sometimes in chess, there are just these blind spots’: Nihal Sarin looks back at his Chess Olympiad loss to Uzbekistan | Exclusive "I'm really not thinking about it," she concluded, laughing. "It's a long way to think. I don't even know whether I'll be playing very actively after two years. I hope, if I could, then I'd be very happy, but the competition at this level is also very high. I'm not even thinking too much further. I just take it tournament by tournament."
Article Summary: Koneru Humpy won two bronze medals at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Board 1 player was under the weather for almost the entirety of the tournament. Humpy produced one of sharpest results of her campaign, a 25-move win over Georgia’s Nana Dzagnidze.

Article Title: 'Not here to be tourists in Argentina': Benin goalkeeper ahead of Lionel Messi's farewell match
Article Text:
Argentina footballer Lionel Messi

‘We are here to compete’

No free goal for Messi

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Benin goalkeeper Marcel Dandjinou has made it clear that Argentina’s farewell celebration for Lionel Messi will not stop his team from competing. As Benin prepare to face Argentina at the Monumental, the 28-year-old goalkeeper says his focus will be on doing his job, even if that means denying Messi a goal on his final night.Dandjinou, who plays for Kruger United in South Africa’s Premier Division, spoke to Spanish newspaper Marca after arriving in Buenos Aires.Despite reports of problems with Benin’s preparations, including claims about poor hotel facilities and difficulties in training, he insisted the team had been treated well."We did not face any problems. We are fine here in Buenos Aires. Why do you say that? The truth is that we have had good conditions," he said.Dandjinou admitted that facing Messi makes the match particularly special, but stressed that Benin are not travelling to Argentina simply to watch the superstar."For me, this match is not like any other match. I think it is an opportunity that will not come again, because it is Messi's last match. It is a special match. But, look, we are here for Argentina and for Messi, but we must not forget that we represent our country too," he added."We are here to defend Benin. This is football: eleven players against eleven. We can win, or draw, or they can win, but it is football. We are not here to be tourists in Argentina; we are here to play and to compete. It will be a great day in our lives."The goalkeeper has huge respect for Messi, having grown up watching him play."For me, Messi is one of football's legends. We grew up watching him play. He is one of our favourite players. To be able to play against him now, on the same pitch, is incredible. I never imagined this would happen, but it will happen on Tuesday. For me, Leo is a legend, a true legend," he further remarked.Asked whether he would allow Messi to score a penalty in the final minutes as a farewell gesture, Dandjinou gave a firm answer."No, no. I am a goalkeeper, and my job is to save the ball. Even if it is the final minute and a penalty is awarded, if Messi takes it, I will try to save it. It is that simple: it is football. Yes, we are here to celebrate Messi, but no one has asked us to give him a goal. And knowing Messi, there is no need to give him anything. If he wants to score, he has to do his best to achieve it," he explained.While every Benin player would love Messi’s shirt, Dandjinou joked that the squad could need plenty of them."If you asked any player in my team, he would tell you he wants his shirt. So it would be great if they made a lot of shirts and gave one to each player. Because if only one of us goes to ask for the shirt, I do not think it will be easy: we all want one," he continued."It would be a great honour for me to play, and that memory will remain engraved in my mind forever. During my career I will be able to say: I was there, in the last match of a legend, in Messi's last match. It is incredible."On the eternal Messi-Cristiano Ronaldo debate, he concluded, "We grew up watching Messi and Cristiano. They taught us a lot about football. They have been competing for a long time. For me, Leo is one of the best players in this sport, indeed one of its kings."
Article Summary: Benin goalkeeper Marcel Dandjinou says his focus will be on doing his job, even if that means denying Messi a goal on his final night. Despite reports of problems with Benin’s preparations, including claims about poor hotel facilities and difficulties in training, he insisted the team had been treated well.

Article Title: In Japan, women’s sumo battles tradition and a male-dominated system for survival
Article Text:
Women sumo wrestlers in Japan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KYOTO: It’s a rainy Sunday morning but that hasn’t stopped more than 100 women and girls from making their way to the Kyoto City Budo Centre, Japan’s oldest martial arts performance hall. Built in 1899, the original structure is mostly out of bounds for visitors. But a recently built adjoining hall is buzzing with activity.The women are dressed in wrestling singlets, wearing the traditional mawashi, the thick belt associated with sumo, over it. At the centre of the hall is a ring that looks like a dohyo, the raised platform on which sumo is contested. It looks like one. But it isn’t.Women are traditionally barred from stepping into a sumo dohyo, a practice rooted in religious beliefs that have long associated menstruation with impurity. Yet, inside this hall, women are doing precisely what tradition has told them they cannot: sumo wrestling.More than 600 women in over 70 clubs practise the traditional form of wrestling in Japan, despite the resistance it has faced. In the wrestling venue at the Asian Games, when a senior official of the Japan Wrestling Association was asked about women’s sumo, he laughed before dismissing it: “It’s no sport for women.”But it wasn’t always this way. Historical research suggests women participated in sumo as far back as the fifth century. The sport also had periods of popularity between 1603 and 1868 and in the early 20th century, before women’s sumo was banned in 1926 on moral and traditional grounds.It returned in organised form in 1997. Yet, amateur women’s sumo continues to fight for survival. The Japan Sumo Association does not recognise it, leaving private clubs, schools and universities to keep it alive.At universities and a few clubs, women train alongside their male counterparts. Even the arrival of Japan’s first female prime minister has not changed the equation. Sanae Takaichi, who became prime minister last year, had said, “I respect tradition. I will not step on the dohyo.”There are, however, women like Airi Hisano, considered the strongest woman sumo wrestler of the country, trying to change things. The 27-yearold Tokyo native began with karate and judo before finding her calling in sumo at Nihon University.She was fortunate to find support at home. “My family wants me to do my best,” she said.It wasn’t easy. “Of course people made fun of me because, in rigid gender spaces, acceptance wasn’t easy. But that didn’t bother me. Also, it wasn’t an Olympic sport,” said Airi, who works in the administrative section of Tachihi Holdings.A heavyweight competitor, Airi balances training with her day job, where she also doubles as a security guard. She holds a third-degree black belt in judo and a first-degree black belt in karate. “We still have a long way to go,” she said.Not far from where Airi was preparing for her bout, Katsumasa Kawase was putting three girls from Team Shiga through their warm-up. “Being a sumo wrestler myself, I didn’t want my daughters to be denied the opportunity when they wanted to try it,” Kawase said, helping his daughters Momoka and Yuzuki warm up.The physical demands are no different from those faced by their male counterparts. The typical diet includes chicken or pork, vegetables, rice and candied sweet potatoes. But muscle is not the biggest hurdle. Awareness is.Morita, who handles public relations for Yoko Sumo Club, an all-women’s team based in Tokyo, said the club was formed in 2024 and has remained exclusively female. “A major challenge is that many people are still unfamiliar with women’s sumo,” she said.What keeps the wrestlers going? “They continue believing that the sport will eventually be included in the Olympics,” Morita said.Women coaches are still few. One of them is Mao Ueda of Hirakata Sumo Club. A former judoka and jiu-jitsu practitioner, she took up coaching after seeing an opportunity to combine her experience in martial arts with the nuances of sumo.“It’s a long road,” she said. The biggest challenge, she believes, comes after university. “With no recognition, money or future, most girls drop out after university. We need a structure to change that,” Ueda said.However, Momoka, 9, knows little about any of that. Two years into the sport, she knows only that she wants to become an Olympian.
Article Summary: More than 600 women in over 70 clubs practise the traditional form of wrestling in Japan. Women are traditionally barred from stepping into a sumo dohyo, a practice rooted in religious beliefs that have long associated menstruation with impurity. Japan Sumo Association does not recognise it, leaving private clubs, schools and universities to keep it alive.

Article Title: Khalid Jamil’s bolder India faces Uruguay as Forlan begins rebuilding after World Cup debacle
Article Text:
Image credit: Indian Football

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: In the past few days, Diego Forlan and his Uruguay team have been staying here like passive guests, happily blending into the background and letting Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil enjoy the public eye. With the departure of their fellow South American rivals, the spotlight is back on La Celeste. So is India’s final act of their extraordinary brush with three World Cup teams in this Fifa international window.Being a football team in transition comes with its own set of challenges. In holding Panama 1-1 and even in losing 0-4 to Brazil, Khalid Jamil’s team has shown glimpses of promise. Teams under Jamil are always known for being defensively strong; sitting deep in numbers is a celebrated way of making life difficult for the opponents. A paradigm shift is now noticeable in the system. India look bolder, more ambitious.“It’s not about me and all credit goes to players,” the former India midfielder told TOI during the pre-match news conference on Monday, the eve of their clash with Uruguay at Salt Lake Stadium.Jamil, however, has warned his players of not repeating the mistakes they had committed against Brazil. “Don’t concede early,” was his advice.Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria in their squad with players equipped with elite mentality. Ranked 20th in the world, they are expected to come hard at the home team with their typical aggression and physicality.Forlan, Golden Ball winner of the 2010 World Cup and an icon in Uruguayan football, also is tasked with rebuilding a team whose World Cup campaigned collapsed into a player revolt against his predecessor Marcelo Bielsa.“I want my players to understand that I’m going to be the same if they win and I’m going to be the same if they lose. But the most important thing is to give your best,” Forlan said in replying to a question from the TOI.“When you win, you’re not the best and when you lose you’re not the worst,” he said.
Article Summary: India take on Uruguay in their final World Cup warm-up match. Khalid Jamil's team have shown glimpses of promise in recent matches. Uruguay have stars like Darwin Nunez, Rodrigo Bentancur, Ronald Araujo and Jose Maria.

Article Title: India 'A' pacers look to step up to the plate against Australia 'A'
Article Text:
India ‘A’ coach Lakshmipathy Balaji and Sai Sudharsan (Image credit: CAP)

PUDUCHERRY: In an era where 350-plus totals in ODIs are becoming the norm, fast bowlers are often left walking a tightrope. India’s recent ODI series against the West Indies was a case in point, with the bowlers conceding 295 and 405 in the first two games before West Indies chased down 352 in the final ODI with 10 balls to spare.As India look towards the 2027 World Cup, where they begin their campaign against Australia on Oct 7, the threematch one-day series between India ‘A’ and Australia ‘A’ in Puducherry offers another window into the country’s pace reserves.The big question is: who can eventually emerge as the ideal partner for Jasprit Bumrah With Arshad Khan , Gurjapneet Singh and Yash Thakur are part of the India ‘A’ setup, it will be interesting to see if anyone can step up.India ‘A’ coach Lakshmipathy Balaji believes the cupboard is far from bare. For him, the answer lies as much in patience and nurturing as it does in raw numbers.“Many have potential. High-scoring games are common now, but bowlers will adapt over time. Bumrah became world-class through time, effort and experience. Youngsters like Anshul (Kamboj) and Gurnoor (Brar) need time and grooming to match international demands. It won’t always be 350-400 run games; bowlers will adapt to modern demands very soon,” Balaji said.Anshul Kamboj was handed his ODI debut in the third game against West Indies after Prasidh Krishna was ruled out. It was, however, a baptism of fire as he conceded 82 runs in nine overs. Gurnoor Brar, who has nine ODIs under his belt, also had an expensive series, while Auqib Nabi went for 84 in 8.5 overs on his ODI debut. Prasidh, too, had a difficult outing in his two games.Yet Balaji does not see the recent run-fests as a cause for concern.“Nothing is lacking, everyone is working hard. Since both teams have scored heavily, batting has temporarily moved ahead of bowling in modern cricket. Once bowling units click together, a balanced contest between bat and ball will return soon,” he said.
Article Summary: India 'A' coach Lakshmipathy Balaji says bowlers will adapt to modern demands. Balaji believes bowlers need time and grooming to match international demands. India begin their 2027 World Cup campaign against Australia on Oct 7 in Puducherry.

Article Title: Up close and personal with Vini & Co? Akash backs teammates
Article Text:
Akash Mishra was in no mood for photos or souvenirs after the 0-4 defeat against Brazil

Kolkata:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India’s historic fixture against five-time world champions Brazil showed even footballers can drop their mask and turn into fans, becoming starry-eyed and awestruck by being in the proximity of players who they have grown up idolising.In about just 50 seconds after the clash at Salt Lake Stadium, more than half of the India team queued up for a prized picture with Vinicius Junior. At last count, there were 14 players who took a quick photograph with the Brazilian star.Others settled for photos with Brazil captain Marquinhos and Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes. The jerseys of Vinicius, captain Marquinhos and Chelsea winger Estevao Willian have also became prized possessions for the India players.“You can show excitement before and after the game, but for 90 minutes (on the field), I feel there was no such (awestruck) behaviour from the boys,” India defender Akash Mishra told TOI on Monday. “I think they tried hard, gave 100%. Yes, after the loss, the mood was not good. But I feel once the final whistle is blown, the excitement comes out. The players have grown up watching them on television (playing for the big clubs).When they got the chance to meet them, I think the excitement was uncontrollable.”Mishra himself was in no mood for photos or souvenirs. Once back at the hotel, he didn’t sleep. Instead, he watched the game all night.“I am a bad loser. Because we lost 4-0, I was not feeling well, and I feel all the boys, they too feel, maybe (they were) not up to the mark. Some of the mistakes which we did were very casual. When we play against such teams, we need to stay focused for 90 minutes,” said Mishra.India lost 4-0 against Brazil in a game the former world champions didn’t appear to take too seriously.Brazil hardly moved out of second gear, scored goals without much of a stretch and coach Carlo Ancelotti made 11 second-half substitutions to give every available player on the Asia Tour a chance.India face Uruguay in another friendly here on Tuesday. The former two-time world champions have high-profile players. There’s Ronald Araujo (Liverpool), Darwin Nunez (Al-Diriyah FC), Jose Maria Gimenez (Atletico Madrid), Rodrigo Bentancur (Tottenham Hotspur) and Mathias Olivera (Napoli).
Article Summary: More than half of the India team queued up for a prized picture with Vinicius Junior. At last count, there were 14 players who took a quick photograph with the Brazilian star. India lost 4-0 against Brazil in a game the former world champions didn't appear to take too seriously.

Article Title: AIFF’s fragile alliance with clubs faces new test
Article Text:
India have twin assignments during the next window in Nov: Two friendlies against World Cuppers New Zealand and the SAFF Championship in Bangladesh

Kolkata:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Everything seems hunky-dory now in the relationship between All India Football Federation (AIFF) and the clubs. India coach Khalid Jamil and the federation have thanked clubs for releasing players ahead of the FIFA window “at a time when they were fine-tuning their squads for the ISL season. ”However, any lingering sense of bonhomie in the proverbial club-versus-country dispute could be a false dawn and the fragile truce between the federation and top-tier clubs is in danger of another breakdown over release of players for the next international window.India have twin assignments during the next window in Nov: Two friendlies against World Cuppers New Zealand and the SAFF Championship in Bangladesh, where India are defending champions. While release of players for the New Zealand assignment will not be an issue, clubs are in no mood to do th same for the SAFF Championship since it’s being played outside the window and overlaps with ISL fixtures.“During the meeting between clubs and Jamil, AIFF made it clear that the priority was the friendlies against New Zealand,” a senior official told TOI. “The friendlies are during the FIFA window (Nov 9-17). The govt is also involved and forms part of a series of sporting events to celebrate ‘100 Years of Unity Through Sport’ between both nations.For SAFF, the fixtures fall outside the window. There is a domestic calendar to be managed too. We are not sure how many clubs will send players and play their fixtures.”The SAFF Championship will be hosted in Dhaka from Nov 4 to 17. Chasing a record-extending tenth SAFF title, India begin their campaign against Maldives on Nov 5, before taking on Pakistan on Nov 11.However, the ISL has released fixtures with matches between Nov 5 and Nov 7. Ten of the 13 clubs will be involved in games when the SAFF Championship is in progress.During the meeting between CEOs of five ISL clubs and Jamil, a tentative probables list was shared for both assignments. While Jamil has named 34 probables for New Zealand friendlies, another list comprises 21 names. The seniors are travelling to New Zealand while a squad comprising under-23 players and reserves — those who don’t make it to the main squad from the 34 — will be on SAFF Championship duty.According to sources, there are players from nine clubs in the first list and ten in the second. Should the list remain untouched, Mohun Bagan and Bengaluru FC will have the maximum players among the probables.
Article Summary: India have twin assignments during the next window in Nov: Two friendlies against World Cuppers New Zealand and the SAFF Championship in Bangladesh. India coach Khalid Jamil has named 34 probables for New Zealand friendlies, another list comprises 21 names.

Article Title: 'Who is the vice-captain?': Basit Ali questions Pakistan cricket selector Aaqib Javed
Article Text:
Aaqib Javed and Salman Agha (Image credit: PCB)

Farhan takes over from Salman

Shaheen remains ODI captain

Pakistan make several squad changes

Pakistan have made several changes to their white-ball teams, but there is still no clarity over who will be the vice-captain in the T20I and ODI sides. Former Pakistan batter Basit Ali has now raised the issue publicly, questioning Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) selector Aaqib Javed about the absence of a vice-captain.Basit took to social media and directly tagged Javed while seeking clarity on the leadership roles in both formats.“T20 and odi ki team mai vice captain khoun hai aqib jawed sb (Who is the vice captain of the T20 and ODI teams, Aaqib Javed sir)”, Basit wrote on X.His question comes after Pakistan made changes to their white-ball leadership ahead of the upcoming series.Sahibzada Farhan has been appointed Pakistan’s new T20I captain, replacing Salman Ali Agha for the three-match series against Sri Lanka. Salman has also been dropped from the T20I squad following the change in leadership.Farhan will lead Pakistan in the T20Is against Sri Lanka on October 9, 11 and 13 in Rawalpindi.The 2026 Asian Games silver medallist recently led Pakistan at the Games, where they lost to India in the final. Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

Article Title: RCA elections face reset? HC hearing PILs tomorrow, fresh polls remain possible
Article Text:

JAIPUR: The Rajasthan Cricket Association (RCA) finds itself trapped in a familiar cycle of political theater and institutional paralysis. What was promised to be a resolution after months of administrative drift has, in true RCA fashion, dissolved into yet another anti-climactic stalemate. Even though the ballots were cast, the Supreme Court’s intervention (order dated Sept 29, 2026), halting the results until the High Court settles pending disputes, leaves the future of Rajasthan cricket suspended in a state of agonising uncertainty.The buildup to the polls exposed power dynamics, revealing deep fractures within the organisation. Initially, the race was a high-stakes standoff between Jodhpur District Cricket Association (DCA) president Dhananjai Singh Khimsar and Churu DCA president Parakram Singh Rathore.If Parakram is to be believed, he had secured the numbers to claim the leadership, commanding a clear majority. However, a directive from the party’s Central leadership made it clear that no politician’s son would head the association. In a move of immediate compliance, Parakram, son of former Leader of Opposition Rajendra Singh Rathore, withdrew from contention and backed Dausa DCA president Brij Kishore Upadhyay in the electoral fray.On the other hand, Dhananjai, son of state health minister Gajendra Singh Khimsar, along with other politicians’ sons, Mohit Yadav (son of BJP MLA Dr Jaswant Singh Yadav) and Ashish Tiwari (son of Rajya Sabha MP Ghanshyam Tiwari ), stood together and decided to fight the elections, confident of their strength. Meanwhile, DD Kumawat, a nominee who later withdrew, took legal counsel and moved the Supreme Court, ultimately prompting the stay on declaring the poll results.Amidst this ongoing turmoil, actual cricket operations have quietly drifted onto autopilot. Current and former players remain conspicuously silent, either accustomed to the political drama or fearful that speaking out could compromise selection or future administrative roles. District officials insist local tournaments continue unhindered, but the systemic uncertainty continues to cast a long shadow over the state's sporting infrastructure.Road ahead & shifting equations: When the Rajasthan High Court resumes hearing the foundational Public Interest Litigation (filed on April 27, 2026) on Wednesday, it will not merely be reviewing the recent election process. Notably, this PIL explicitly demands that strict action be taken against non-compliant ad hoc committee members for their failure to hold elections on time, including their removal from their respective district cricket associations. Under the SC’s mandate, the HC is set to address the entire matrix of pending challenges in one unified proceeding.“This means the court will simultaneously examine the accountability and eligibility of those who were a part of the different ad hoc panels formed over the period of two and half years, recent petitions demanding mandated female representation in RCA governance, and the legitimacy of voting rights granted to newly added or previously suspended district associations,” explained a lawyer tracking the RCA development.Observers note that the legal battle could swing in several different directions. On one hand, there is a distinct possibility that the issue could be resolved quickly by the High Court. Insiders suggest that if the court clears the current voting process without delay, the government-backed Upadhyay & Co is heavily favoured to win, given that sources claim they have at least 30 votes firmly in their favour.Conversely, the hearings could drag on much longer than originally expected, prolonged by the sheer volume of cross-petitions and constitutional objections, which would leave the association in prolonged administrative limbo.Adding to the legal entanglement, an RCA insider also pointed out how there was no ombudsman appointed for the elections, which goes directly against the Lodha Panel recommendations. "According to the Lodha Committee rules, having an active Ombudsman is a prerequisite for a legally compliant election process," he added, highlighting another structural flaw that could compromise the validity of the polls.If the High Court rules that former ad hoc members face a conflict of interest or disqualification due to non-compliance, key contenders like Dhananjai, Mohit, and Ashish could be ruled out. If that happens, or if the court scraps the recent voting to order fresh elections altogether, the entire arithmetic alters dramatically.In the event of fresh elections, the dynamic between Parakram and Upadhyay will face an immediate test. Instead of simply stepping aside for Upadhyay, Parakram may rethink his decision and re-enter the race for the president’s post. He could launch a fresh effort to lobby top party leaders for explicit backing, arguing that changed legal parameters alter his position,” said an RCA insider, closely monitoring the election dynamics.Such a move would directly threaten Upadhyay’s presidential ambitions, setting the stage for a tense internal power struggle within their faction.

Even though the ballots were cast, the Supreme Court’s intervention (order dated Sept 29, 2026) halting the results until the High Court settles pending disputes.

MUMBAI: In another huge boost to his fledgling career and a vote of confidence in his abilities, Mumbai's senior selection committee, led by Rajesh Pawar, on Monday appointed opener Ayush Mhatre as the new vice-captain of Mumbai’s Ranji Trophy squad for the first match of the 2026-27 season against Chandigarh from Oct 11 at the Wankhede Stadium, even as they snubbed India's 2026 T20 World Cup winning captain Suryakumar Yadav , who had earlier confirmed his availability and willingness to be a part of Mumbai's Ranji side, on the grounds that he needed to "play more red-ball cricket."The 16-member squad, which will be captained by veteran batter Siddhesh Lad , includes India's Test opener Yashasvi Jaiswal and Sarfaraz Khan.The 36-year-old Suryakumar didn't feature in any of pre-season tournaments for Mumbai, the local Kanga League, and didn't take part in the in Mumbai's intra-squad matches at the Brabourne Stadium and the MCA's ground in BKC recently."If Surya were to be picked, Musheer Khan, who scored 96 for West Zone in the Duleep Trophy in Aug, would have had to be dropped. That wasn't feasible," a source in the Mumbai Cricket Association told TOI.The selection committee was attended by former India skipper Dilip Vengsarkar, who is the MCA's Cricket Advisor."Surya is available but it was thought to go with the youngsters for the time being. He is obviously a big-match player and a proven performer for Mumbai. We just want to get into rhythm by playing a few red-ball matches. Surya hasn’t played a red-ball match for the last 18 months, so we want him to have a few games under his belt and then he can get into the team," Pawar told reporters.Throwing light on the appointment of Lad and Mhatre as the new captain and vice-captain of the Mumbai team, Pawar said, "The selection committee unanimously has gone with experienced Siddhesh Lad as the captain for the seasons. Along with a senior, we have planned to groom a junior in Ayush as the vice-captain. He has led the India Under-19 to the (U-19) World Cup win, is a smart cricketer and is in excellent nick."TOI had reported about veteran seam bowling allrounder Shardul Thakur suffering from a hand injury during a practice match at the Cricket Club of India after being struck by a ball hit by Mhatre and is likely to miss a few matches initially of Mumbai's 2026-27 Ranji Trophy campaign. We played four-day games at the KSCA Invitational and then played in Puducherry as well. This is our best team and the youngsters have also come in on the back of excellent performances and the seasoned players are in-form for India A and Duleep Trophy.A notable omission was young opener Angkrish Raghuvanshi, who recently scored a double century (203) for Rest of India Under-23 team against CK Nayudu Trophy champions Tamil Nadu on the weekend. LUCKNOW: Coming off the golden glow of their Asian Games triumph in Japan, India step into Tuesday’s fivematch T20I series opener against the West Indies at the Ekana Stadium here carrying momentum, silverware and an intriguing selection headache at the top of the order.While Abhishek Sharma’s explosive presence as a designated opener is virtually etched in ink, the suspense lies in who walks out alongside him. It is a clash of narratives: the breathtaking audacity of youth versus the hardened composure of experience.In one corner stands teen prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, whose fearless strokeplay has set pulses racing across the circuit. In the other is Sanju Samson , the seasoned campaigner whose heroics in India’s 2026 T20 World Cup triumph remains etched in cricketing folklore.Will head coach Gautam Gambhir lean into the romance of the next generation, or will he trust the calm authority of a proven match-winner?Bowling coach Morne Morkel acknowledged the delicate juggling act ahead of the first T20I. “I’m pretty sure Gautam will look to rotate him (Sooryavanshi). That is up to the selectors, and the coach and the captain, in terms of the playing level, or which playing level will be the best to win a game for India on our home soil.In terms of the starting X, he guys just came back from an Asian Games, so we’re going to see how everybody’s feeling after jet lag, after travelling, and then from there, make plans accordingly. ”Fatigue, indeed, remains a tangible hurdle. “The red flag, or the problem, might be our guys travelling back and then immediately playing an international match after the Asian Games,” Morkel said. “Some of the guys arrived only a couple of days ago. But I think once we are up and running, and the series gets going, we will be up for it.”The spotlight will also be on skipper Shreyas Iyer . Iyer’s blade yielded just 34 runs across two Asian Games fixtures and 48 in three matches against Afghanistan.Fortunately for India, their bowling arsenal welcomes back two electrifying local favourites returning to action after the Zimbabwe tour in July: Mayank Yadav and Prince Yadav.Standing in India’s way is a dangerous West Indies outfit marshalled by Shai Hope, who is in blistering touch following back-to-back ODI centuries.For the Caribbean side, Lucknow is a familiar venue. Though history has rarely been kind to them, yielding just one win and three losses in four T20Is at the venue compared to India’s dominant 3-1 ledger.

Article Title: 'We all have huge sympathy': Why England cricket ready to fund West Indies Test

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) could step in financially if needed to ensure England’s women play a Test in the West Indies next spring. The match is planned as part of a multi-format series and is considered important preparation for England’s 2027 Ashes campaign.Cricket West Indies (CWI) recently announced several cost-cutting measures, including reductions in player contracts. Earlier this year, it also cancelled a planned women’s Test against Australia, although the rest of that tour went ahead.There have been no talks about cancelling England’s Test, and the wider tour, which includes three T20s and three ODIs, is not currently under threat.Speaking to the BBC, ECB chair Richard Thompson said: "I hope not. That's not expected to be cancelled. I hope it will take place."He also said the ECB would "look at" providing financial help if CWI faced difficulties staging the match.Normally, the host cricket board pays the costs of hosting visiting teams. However, touring in the Caribbean can be expensive because players often need to travel between different islands. CWI said it has spent more than $80m on domestic air travel over the past 15 years.Thompson said the ECB wants the Test to happen because England need more red-ball cricket before the Ashes."We want that Test match to play out," said Thompson. "It's very important for us because our first women's match in the Ashes is the Headingley Test, so we need a good red-ball warm-up."We've got to be playing somewhere and we'd much prefer that to be the West Indies."England have played just one Test since their Ashes defeat in early 2025, losing to India at Lord’s. They have not faced West Indies in a women’s Test since 1979, while West Indies last played a Test in 2004.England will also hold a 10-day red-ball training camp in India in January as part of their Ashes preparations.Thompson added: "We all have a huge sympathy for the West Indies, we all want to see a successful West Indian nation. They have very unique challenges and I hope through the International Cricket Council and others we can find a way through this."

Shaheen Shah Afridi will continue to captain the ODI side in the upcoming tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka.Shaheen Shah Afridi (captain), Abrar Ahmed, Arafat Minhas, Babar Azam, Faheem Ashraf, Fakhar Zaman, Haris Rauf, Hasan Nawaz, Muhammad Ghazi Ghori (wk), Naseem Shah, Razaullah, Saad Baig (wk), Saim Ayub, Salman Ali Agha, Shadab Khan and Sufiyan Moqim.Pakistan will begin their upcoming assignments with the three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi.The T20I series will be followed by a seven-match ODI tri-series involving Pakistan, England and Sri Lanka. The tournament will begin in Rawalpindi before moving to Lahore, where the final four matches, including the final, will be played.
Article Summary: Pakistan to play three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka. Sahibzada Farhan named new captain for T20Is. Salman Ali Agha left out of ODI squad. Shaheen Shah Afridi will continue to captain ODI side.

Article Title: Vithya Ramraj on newfound fame: 'I'm still far away from reaching world standards'

CHENNAI: With three medals and newfound recognition, Vithya Ramraj returned home from the Asian Games with plenty to celebrate. People at petrol bunks, airports and bus stands have started recognizing her, but it has left the 28-year old, who broke P T Usha’s 400 metre 42-year-old hurdles record, slightly surprised.“People are recognising me now and I’m happy athletics is growing. I’m also thinking about the recognition I am getting. Is it because of the relay medals or because I broke the record? Why have I become famous? That is one constant thing on my mind. I’m still far away from reaching world standards, and my coach was not happy with the timing.“Personally, I didn’t get the satisfaction even though people celebrated. I think of how Neeraj Chopra is celebrated, and if I reach his level, then more people will know me,” Vithya told TOI.What worked for Vithya in 400m hurdles was that she brought down her stride count from 17 to 16 between hurdles 5 and 6.“In the bend from the fifth to the sixth hurdle, I used to take 17 strides, but I have now reduced it to 16. We have been working on it since Nov last year. That helped me going into the home stretch.”Going into the Asian Games, Vithya did not dip below 56 seconds even once this season. While she bagged gold at the Federation Cup and Inter-state athletics meet, her coach Nehpal Singh, who has been a strong source of support, was not satisfied with the medals.“My coach told me, ‘Did I train you to run 56 seconds? What performance have you put in?’”What Vithya felt helped her in the run-up to the Asian Games was the training stints she had in Poland and the Czech Republic with Nehpal.“I used to sleep for 10 hours for three months during the stint abroad, but in India, I used to sleep only for 7-8 hours. In India, I cannot train at 10 am due to the climate, but the sleep cycle in Poland helped me. In India, I train from 5:30am to 8:30am,” she said.

Article Title: EXCLUSIVE | 'Fear may never completely go away': Sujeet Kalkal on turning Olympic heartbreak into Asian Games gold
Article Text:
Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI)

Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI)

Sujeet Kalkal during his gold medal bout (Image credit: PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
