NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour.On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics.Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games.The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title.When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile.For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold."This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him.The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target."Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said.And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [“If you’re going to the Olympics, don’t go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]."India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph."India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said.The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence.After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds.The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout.Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all.Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title."The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said.Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey."I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said.The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024."Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said."Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said.The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms."Gold ke liye jaana hai."
Article Summary: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport. He was on his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an Asian Games gold. He fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev.

Article Title: Other side of India's Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
Article Text:
AP Photo

The spending breakdown

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s 85-medal haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games was its secondbest finish, but the headline numbers don’t reveal everything.A sport-by-sport audit by TOI shows that 137 Indian athletes across 16 disciplines returned empty-handed, exposing persistent gaps in the country’s medal ambitions.India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.Yet 137 athletes across 16 disciplines won nothing.Another 64 athletes across six sports managed six bronze — one each in kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and wushu. The zero-medal list included canoeing (19 athletes), cycling (14), equestrian (7), esports (15), fencing (20), gymnastics (1), judo (3), karate (2), rugby sevens (13), sport climbing (2), surfing (4), swimming (12), taekwondo (3), tennis (7), teqball (3) and volleyball (12). The six-bronze group comprised kurash (6 athletes), MMA (2), rowing (22), sepaktakraw (21), soft tennis (6) and wushu (7).In all, 201 athletes accounted for just six bronze medals across the 22 disciplines mentioned above. In other prominent sports with sizable athlete numbers, table tennis sent 10 athletes and returned with one bronze and badminton’s 20-member contingent managed one bronze in the men’s team event.Together, the two sent 37 athletes and produced only two bronze.India contested in 259 medal events in AichiNagoya and won medals in just 20, a 7.7% eventpodium conversion rate. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%.The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle (Nov 2023-Aug 2026), led by badminton (Rs 49.26 cr), cycling track (Rs 35.9 cr), fencing (Rs 28.2 cr), table tennis (Rs 25.3 cr), tennis (Rs 22.4 cr) and canoe/kayak (Rs 20.1 cr). Other allocations included rowing (Rs 13.8 cr,) swimming (Rs 10.8 cr), gymnastics (Rs 10.49 cr), judo (Rs 8.05 cr), wushu (Rs 7.8 cr), volleyball (Rs 6.5 cr), sepaktakraw (Rs 5.7 cr), equestrian (Rs 3.7 cr), rugby (Rs 3.63 cr), surfing (Rs 2.9 cr), karate (Rs 1.99 cr), soft tennis (Rs 1.6 cr) and kurash (Rs 1.6 cr).On three sports – MMA, eSports and sport climbing, the govt spent no money. As per the govt’s own estimates, it spent approximately Rs 703 cr across 30 disciplines during the Nov 2023-Aug 2026 preparation cycle. The Rs 703 cr included about Rs 118 cr for domestic training and national coaching camps, Rs 40 cr for overseas training, Rs 252 cr for international competition exposure, Rs 89 cr for equipment, Rs 86 cr for foreign coaches/support staff and Rs 118 cr for other expenses, including Indian experts, championships, competitions in India, grassroots and coach development.Also, a total of 427 athletes who were part of the govt’s various programmes and schemes participated in the Games, including 77 athletes from Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) Core group, 78 from TOPS Development 78, 48 from Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), 65 Khelo India Athlete (KIA), 25 from National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) and 134 from National Coaching Camps (NCCs).The Glasgow comparison is revealing, though not like-for-like. India had 122 athletes and para-athletes in 10 sports at the curtailed 2026 Commonwealth Games and won 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze — also finishing fourth. The Asian Games contingent was 4.06 times larger, but its 85-medal haul was only 2.18 times Glasgow’s. Medal efficiency was 17.2 per 100 athletes in Aichi-Nagoya against 32 in Glasgow.The message is that at this level, the medal base remains concentrated.For a country investing Rs 703 cr across a multi-year cycle, the next challenge is clear: turn wider participation, exposure and support into wider podium conversion.
Article Summary: India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%. The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current Asian Games cycle.

Article Title: World champion beaten, Olympic champion toppled at Asian Games: Wrestlers dream of hearing India’s national anthem at the LA Olympics
Article Text:
India's gold-medallist wrestlers - Sujeet Kalkal and Aman Sehrawat.

Sehrawat turns a difficult phase into gold

Aman Sehrawat

Kalkal follows gold with an Olympic-sized ambition

India's Sujeet Kalkal, right, competes in the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

From selling milk to a historic Greco-Roman final

Nitesh Siwach (Image credit: X)

Punia battles through a new weight category

Deepak Punia (ANI Photo)

Panghal improves on Hangzhou, Kumar makes history

Antim Panghal

Six medals, one bigger dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze — and a much bigger target already occupying their minds: the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver and Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze.The campaign was also marked by two major statements. Sehrawat defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song in the men's 57kg freestyle final, while Kalkal beat Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka on his way to gold in the 65kg category.For the Indian wrestlers, however, Nagoya was less about looking back at what they had achieved and more about building towards what comes next.For Sehrawat, the gold was the culmination of one of the most difficult phases of his young career.The 23-year-old had won bronze at the Paris Olympics but subsequently struggled with motivation in 2025. A persistent stomach ailment also forced him to miss important competitions.In Nagoya, however, Sehrawat rediscovered his best. He defeated reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the final, recovering after the North Korean had turned a 1-6 deficit into a 7-6 lead.It was Sehrawat's first Asian Games gold after his bronze at Hangzhou."Ups and downs, injuries keep happening like this. That phase also comes, but I had the belief in my mind. We should never give up, and I did the same. Today, I have won a gold medal in the Games. The future goal is the Olympics," Sehrawat said after returning to India.He said the next goal was to replicate the achievement on the biggest stage."We won gold for the country. The plan for the future is exactly the same — we will win gold for the country and prepare accordingly. I thank all the countrymen; it was their prayers that worked in the matches," he added.Then came the statement that perhaps best captured the mood of India's wrestling contingent."...now we will do better in the future. The whole nation is giving us love. Now our national anthem will be played at the LA Olympics."If Sehrawat's gold was a comeback story, Kalkal's was a lesson in refusing to surrender.The world No. 2 entered the Asian Games unbeaten this season and lived up to his billing in the men's 65kg freestyle category.Before the final, Kalkal defeated Japan's Olympic champion Kiyooka and Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi. Against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final, he appeared to be heading towards defeat after falling 2-9 behind.Instead, he produced a stunning late comeback to win 10-9.The victory restored India's hold on the 65kg Asian Games title, a category in which Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia had previously won gold."Whatever struggle I did has paid off. The final match was tough, but I was only thinking of winning that time," Kalkal said.His sights are already firmly fixed on Los Angeles."Now we will practice more, and if all goes well, we will win gold at the Olympics too. For the Olympics, the practice has already begun," Kalkal added.Nitesh Siwach's silver carried perhaps the most remarkable backstory of India's six medallists.A serious knee injury as a teenager kept him away from wrestling for more than 18 months. During that period, he helped his family with its dairy business and sold milk in Panipat.His comeback culminated in an historic Asian Games final appearance in the men's 97kg Greco-Roman category — India's first in the weight class in 64 years.Siwach eventually lost 0-4 to Japan's Yuri Nakazato but returned home with a silver medal and a clear Olympic target."I feel great. This is the first time I am getting such respect and honour. I am experiencing such a great welcome for the first time, and I am very happy," he said. "I had aimed for gold. I didn't win gold, but I did secure the silver medal and I am very happy about that. Since this was my first Asian Games, I am delighted with the silver."Siwach also believes India's Greco-Roman wrestlers can make their presence felt in Los Angeles."People used to say we wouldn't win medals in Greco-Roman, but we will continue to excel. We will bring home medals from the Los Angeles Olympics," he said.His personal target is even clearer."I made some mistakes, which is why I had to settle for silver. My goal going forward is to win gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and I will work extremely hard for it," he added.He has already begun that preparation."My preparation for the Olympics has already begun, starting from the very day I won the medal. I have to bring a gold in the Olympics," Siwach said.Deepak Punia's bronze was another product of perseverance.The 2019 World Championships silver medallist had competed at 86kg and 92kg before moving to 97kg this year following a muscle injury.Despite the challenges of changing weight categories, Punia earned selection for the Asian Games and defeated Mongolia's Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 2-1 in the bronze-medal bout."Winning a medal was quite challenging for me because I used to compete in the 86kg category, but this time I participated in the 97kg category. There were many challenges, and my hope and goal was to win the gold medal. However, I had to settle for the bronze," Punia said.Experience helped him deal with the pressure."I have been playing for a long time, so there is pressure; there is pressure on every athlete. But I understood how I had to handle the pressure. In my mind, it was just that I had to give my best. It was not like I had to take over-pressure. I just had to give my 100 per cent and that's what I did," he said.Antim Panghal also upgraded her medal from bronze at Hangzhou to silver in the women's 53kg category.She lost 1-9 to Japan's Moe Kiyooka in the final after coaches had worked on keeping her calm and confident before the competition."It is my second time winning a medal. But I had thought that I had to come first, but I could not come first. In the future, I will try to do better than this," Panghal said.Sunil Kumar, meanwhile, returned to the podium after knee surgery to win bronze in the men's 87kg Greco-Roman category. He defeated the Philippines' Callum Johnston Roberts 9-0 by technical superiority, becoming the first Indian Greco-Roman wrestler to win two Asian Games medals after his bronze at Hangzhou."I am very happy and want to thank all my fellow countrymen. May your blessings and support continue to be with me," Kumar said.The six medals tell only part of India’s wrestling story in Nagoya.Sehrawat battled through a difficult phase to defeat a reigning world champion. Kalkal stunned an Olympic champion before producing a remarkable comeback for gold. Siwach overcame a serious teenage injury and years of struggle to reach a historic Greco-Roman final. Punia changed weight categories and still made the podium, while Panghal improved her medal colour and Kumar returned from knee surgery to make history.But beyond the six medals was a bigger message — India’s wrestlers are already looking towards Los Angeles.Their words after returning home reflected an ambition that goes far beyond Nagoya: to turn this success into Olympic gold in 2028.
Article Summary: Aman Sehrawat and Sujeet Kalkal struck gold, while Nitesh Siwach and Antim Panghal won silver. Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar added bronze. India's wrestlers arrived in Aichi-Nagoya carrying questions over injuries, form and confidence. They left with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze.

Article Title: From ending South Korea’s reign to booking 2028 LA Olympics quotas: Indian archers return from Asian Games with bigger target
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

‘We proved exactly what they’re made of’

Gold medallists India's Chikitha Taniparthi and Sahil Rajesh Jadhav celebrate after winning the Compound Mixed Team Final. (Reuters Photo)

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod in action. (Reuters Photo)

‘We thought that we would do it, and we did’

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate after winning the gold medal. (Reuters Photo)

Bigger target: LA 2028

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's archers returned home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. They came back with history rewritten, Olympic qualification secured and the belief that the gap with the world's best is narrowing rapidly.The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya, with both the compound and recurve squads producing landmark performances. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place, while the recurve women's team ended South Korea's long-standing dominance by beating the 10-time Olympic champions 5-3 in the final.For a group that had faced questions before the Games, the response was emphatic. India's compound coach Dave Cousins believes the performance should put those doubts to rest.Cousins said the coaching group had deliberately avoided making medal predictions before the Games, instead focusing on preparation and execution.“So early on, they wanted us to make predictions on how many medals we could get. The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could,” Cousins said.The results, he argued, were a reflection of a stronger support system around the archers.“When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. So we're very happy with that. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now,” he added.The success was particularly significant because much of the compound squad was relatively inexperienced on the biggest international stage.“You in the media and the global archery community really had a lot of questions about our younger archers, the new squad. Well, I think we proved exactly what they're made of,” Cousins said.Jadhav and Taniparthu were at the heart of that response. Their mixed-team gold not only delivered another Asian Games title but also secured India's Olympic quota place.Jadhav said the final against Chinese Taipei was less about pressure and more about sticking to a plan repeatedly rehearsed in training.“It feels fantastic, and seeing this grand welcome gives us even more joy. There wasn't pressure as such because we had practised specifically for these situations,” Jadhav said. “It was all about execution, and we delivered. Now I feel all the hard work I've put in so far has truly paid off.”Taniparthu said the victory had given the young group another reason to work harder.“This feels so good and happy, and by this we will get motivated that we have to win more, do more hard work, then every time we will also get this,” she said.The compound women's team also underlined India's growing strength by equalling the world record score during its 238-234 victory over China. Taniparthu won that gold alongside veteran Jyothi Surekha Vennam and Prithika Pradeep.Sahil was also part of the men's gold-medal-winning team, while Ganesh Mani Ratnam Thirumuru won men's team gold and individual bronze. Kushal Dalal was another member of the men's gold-winning side.The recurve contingent produced its own piece of history.Kumkum Mohod emerged as one of India's biggest individual stars, winning women's individual gold and helping the country secure women's team gold and mixed team silver. Her individual triumph also secured an Olympic quota for India.The 17-year-old said the result was the product of collective preparation rather than an individual effort.“What we thought would happen, happened. It was the team's hard work, all the team's motivation, and the support of the Archery Association of India and SAI. That's why everything happened,” she said.In the individual final against South Korea's Oh Yejin, Kumkum consciously shut out the opponent and concentrated on her own shooting.“In the final match, I completely enjoyed my shooting. I held on to my feeling, just shot my arrows and didn't look at who was ahead,” she said.Her advice after the breakthrough was equally simple.“Just stay disciplined and do your best at your work. Don't get carried away. Just keep doing your work properly,” she added.But it was the women's team victory over 10-time Olympic champions South Korea that arguably carried the biggest historical significance. Kirti Sharma was part of the side that defeated the Koreans 5-3, ending their dominance in the event.“India's first gold in this event. We beat Korea to win gold, so this created history for us. I feel very good that I was part of the team that created that history,” Sharma said.The magnitude of the challenge was not lost on the Indian team.“There was pressure because that team always took gold, so there was pressure on us, but we thought that we would do it, and we did,” Sharma said.The men's recurve squad also contributed to India's medal haul, with Dhiraj Bommadevara winning silver in the mixed team event with Kumkum and another silver in the men's team event. Neeraj Chauhan claimed individual bronze and men's team silver, while Yashdeep Bhoge was part of the silver-winning men's team.Bommadevara believes the support structure around Indian archery has changed dramatically.“Earlier, there was hardly any support, and I relied closely on my family and friends. But if it weren't for this government, I wouldn't be standing here today. Our Prime Minister, our Sports Minister and our administrative setup have been so supportive,” he said.The pressure of an Asian Games, he added, was easier to manage because of the team's environment.“Pressure is there for everyone, but we were fortunate to have a team where we could stay cool and calm,” he said.And the next targets are already visible.“Next year, we have the World Championships, where Olympic quotas are there, and after that the LA Olympics,” he said.For Chauhan, the Asian Games was his first experience of the multi-sport event, and the medal made the occasion even more meaningful.“Overall, the experience of the Asian Games was very good. It was my first Asian Games. I went with the hope that I had to bring a medal for India, and bringing this medal has made me and my family very proud,” he said.Bhoge, making his debut, highlighted the collective spirit that helped India navigate the crucial moments.“Obviously it was my debut, so there were crunch moments, but everyone kept their morale up. The team stayed together. Because the whole team stayed together, we were able to play well and maintain ourselves,” he said.The Asian Games medals have therefore brought celebration, but also a bigger expectation. With Olympic quotas secured, South Korea's recurve dominance finally broken and a new generation of compound archers announcing themselves, India's archery programme now has a new benchmark.The Aichi-Nagoya triumph was historic. The next target is bigger — Los Angeles 2028.
Article Summary: India's archers return home from the Asian Games with more than a record medal haul to celebrate. The Indian contingent collected five gold, two silver and two bronze medals in Aichi-Nagoya. The compound mixed team of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthu secured an Olympic quota place.

The Asian Games 2026 took place in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4, with athletes from 46 nations competing across various sports. India finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals, including 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes.India enjoyed several memorable performances, with the men’s and women’s teams winning gold medals in cricket, kabaddi and hockey. It was also the first time both Indian hockey teams won gold at the same Asian Games Among the standout individual performers was 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold.She finished the Games with two golds and a silver. Pranavi Urs also created history by winning India’s first individual golf gold, while Neeru Dhanda became the country’s first women’s trap shooting gold medallist.At just 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi became India’s youngest-ever Asian Games gold medallist. The teenage batting sensation was part of the Indian men’s cricket team that defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final to win gold.Sooryavanshi made an aggressive start, hitting two consecutive sixes, before Saim Ayub dismissed him for 15 off nine balls. Despite his early exit, India went on to win the final and secure a memorable gold medal.Two-time Olympian Mairaj Ahmad Khan became India’s oldest medallist at the 2026 Asian Games at the age of 50. He won bronze as part of the men’s skeet shooting team alongside Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Bhavtegh Singh Gill.Khan has competed internationally for more than 20 years and is a three-time ISSF World Cup gold medallist. However, the bronze in Aichi-Nagoya was his first Asian Games medal.Overall, Japan’s 11-year-old eSports player Yuki Kurihara became the youngest gold medallist in Asian Games history after winning the Puyo Puyo Champions title. Kuwait’s 63-year-old shooter Abdullah Al-Rashidi was the oldest medallist overall, winning silver in men’s skeet.
Article Summary: The Asian Games 2026 took place in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4. India finished fourth in the medal table with 85 medals, including 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes. Among the standout individual performers was 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold.

Article Title: 'It's like water to a thirsty person': Asian Games gold reignites women's hockey at grassroots
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

KOLKATA: The Indian women’s hockey team’s Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics.According to coaches who have nurtured generations of players across the country, the triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport while validating decades of hard work in academies and training centres, far from the spotlight.Former India captain Pritam Siwach, who has been working as a coach for more than 25 years in Sonipat, Haryana, believes the impact of the victory extends well beyond the podium.“This victory has given women’s hockey a new lease of life. It is like giving water to a thirsty person. Winning gold after 44 years has ended a long drought and brought renewed energy to the sport,” she said, adding that the success has given women’s hockey the recognition it deserves after years of operating in the shadow of the men’s game.For coaches working at the grassroots level, the medal has become a powerful tool. Dasrath Mahato, the 69-year-old from Khunti in Jharkhand who discovered and mentored Nikki Pradhan, said every major success creates a ripple effect among young athletes.“When children see players returning home with medals, they start to believe they can do the same. It inspires them to work harder and pursue hockey seriously,” Mahato said.The success has also been celebrated by coaches who have worked in some of the country’s leading hockey centres. Madhya Pradesh Hockey Academy coach Vandana says achievements at the elite level invariably strengthen the grassroots ecosystem.“When a sport performs well at the top level, it benefits the grassroots. We are already seeing more academies and leagues being established for women, and success like this will only accelerate that growth,” said Vandana, who trained the likes of Sushila Chanu and Bichu Devi Kharibam.Former India goalkeeper and coach Edgar Mascarenhas, who worked extensively in Odisha, described the achievement as one of the biggest milestones in the history of Indian women’s hockey.“I watched every match and what impressed me most was their fighting spirit. Even in difficult situations, they never gave up,” said Mascarenhas.The direct Olympic qualification has also been highlighted as one of the competition’s biggest outcomes. Coaches unanimously agreed that avoiding the pressure of an additional qualification campaign allows the team to focus entirely on preparation for the Games.“This may actually be even more important than the gold medal itself,” said Siwach. “Now the players know they are going to the Olympics and can devote all their energy towards preparing for that challenge.”The impact has been felt in regions that have emerged as strong contributors to Indian women’s hockey. In Mizoram, where coach Miss Btei helped nurture internationals Lalremsiami and Lalthantluangi, interest in the sport continues to grow among young children.“The success of players from our state will encourage more youngsters to take up hockey. Children see what Lalremsiami has achieved and begin to believe they can follow the same path,” she said.According to Btei, players as young as nine or ten years old, are now entering the development pathway with the latest generation already benefiting from the visibility created by the national team’s success.For former India international and coach Ajit Lakra, the gold medal represents proof that India’s grassroots structures are delivering results.“These players came through the grassroots system and delivered a gold-medal performance that resonated across Asia. It shows young athletes that there is a pathway from the grassroots level to the international stage,” said Lakra, who coached Rutuja Dadaso Pisal.While they welcomed the growing number of opportunities for women, the coaches stressed the importance of greater investment in infrastructure, academies and player development programmes to sustain the momentum.Yet the overriding sentiment remains one of optimism. Whether in hockey strongholds like Jharkhand and Odisha, established academies in Madhya Pradesh or emerging centres like Mizoram, coaches see the medal as a catalyst for growth.
Article Summary: The Indian women's hockey team's Asian Games gold medal after a 44-year wait has done more than secure direct qualification for the Olympics. The triumph has rekindled belief at the grassroots, and is destined to inspire a new generation of girls to take up the sport.

Article Title: The road to LA 2028: How Sjoerd Marijne and his team rebuilt India's women's hockey side
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

At the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium, tears flowed freely on the pitch. More than 5,500km away, in India, women’s hockey’s loyal legion, small in numbers but deep in investment, rejoiced.They had watched a team in which skill was matched by fitness, individual brilliance was backed by teamwork and, finally, belief had returned.The gold medal, won after 44 years, was defining. But the direct ticket to the Los Angeles Olympics was unprecedented.Interest in women’s hockey had gathered pace after India’s fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics. Missing out on Paris, however, dented the hopes and aspirations that had begun to build.Then came the well-documented rifts, allegations, a dip in form and a spate of injuries. The shadow over Los Angeles grew darker.Enter Sjoerd Marijne and his support staff. They did not have a magic wand to make the demons disappear. What they brought was a systematic approach to rebuilding the physical and psychological framework of the team.The Dutchman was quick to point out that rebuilding a team is never the work of one person.“There’s a great connection among the staff and the players. I’m doing the interviews, but it’s an achievement from the whole staff. I’m really happy with all the quality I have around me,” he said.But there was another requirement, ensuring the players were fit enough to play as one.That was where Wayne Lombard, the team’s head of athletic performance, came in. He had a broad idea of the physical state of the squad when he arrived.The support staff hit the reset button. Rodet Yila and Caira Yila were brought in as scientific advisers, while the immediate priority was not fitness for fitness’ sake, but getting the players healthy.“Regardless of what the fitness levels were, the priority was to address the injury concerns,” Lombard said.That required more than exercises and numbers. The players had to believe in the process.“We had to sit down with the players and earn their buy-in. Helping them understand that the physical side of the game is every bit as important as the technical and tactical side,” Lombard said.He introduced the 30-15 intermittent fitness test to establish the players’ maximum aerobic speed. The test required them to run for 30 seconds, rest for 15 and progress across a 40m grid, with the speed increasing by 0.5kmph at every stage.Muscle by muscle, the players rebuilt their strength. With it came confidence.As the year progressed, India began to look increasingly like a team t rather than a collection of talented individuals.Poetic justice or coincidence, Japan had stood in India’s way in the qualifiers for the Paris Olympics. In Japan, a little over two years later, India cleared the hurdle to Los Angeles.
Article Summary: The gold medal, won after 44 years, was defining. But the direct ticket to the Los Angeles Olympics was unprecedented. Sjoerd Marijne and his support staff brought a systematic approach to rebuilding the physical and psychological framework of the team.

Article Title: Asian Games: Japan signs off, Doha takes the 2030 baton

NAGOYA: It has been a testing three weeks for Japan. Accommodation woes, transport and logistical nightmares, mismanagement and weather that refused to cooperate – the challenges the Asian Games organisers faced were plenty.Yet, as the Games drew to a close, there was enough to celebrate. Records were broken, medals won, friendships forged and, on Sunday, the baton was passed to Doha as Japan bid farewell to representatives from 44 countries at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium.India finished fourth in the medals tally, while China topped the standings by a distance, collecting 341 medals, including an astonishing 169 golds.Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani described the Games as an event that would “shape the next generation of Asian sport” before welcoming the next chapter to his home country.“Tonight, as we lower the flag on Aichi-Nagoya 2026, we close these Games, but we raise the bar for Asian sport,” he said.“Over 350 records have been broken, including more than 50 world records. Forty out of the 45 NOCs achieved medals. This is a record for our Asian Games,” the 40-year-old added.In a symbolic handover to the next hosts, Qatar’s equestrian rider Jassim Al Kuwari, entered the stadium on horseback and received the OCA flag on behalf of Doha, which will host the 2030 Games.

Article Title: New beginnings, new heroes: Women lead India's charge as a new generation shines in Nagoya
Article Text:
Lovlina Borgohain and Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: X)

The comeback girls

Golden standards

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As Neeru Dhanda led the Indian contingent out for one last time at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on Sunday night, it was symbolic of how India’s Asian Games campaign had unfolded over the past two weeks.The women had come to the fore - packing punches, vaulting to new heights, lifting weights, taking aim, towering over opponents with sixes, blazing the track, finding the fairway and hitting the back of the net. India’s final tally of 85 medals, including 21 gold, may represent a drop from the 106 medals and 28 golds won in Hangzhou. But numbers alone cannot tell the story of these Games.There were path-breakers everywhere, athletes who pushed through glass ceilings that had stood for years. The aftermath will bring reviews, reflections, deliberations and reports. But before the analysis begins, it is only fair to celebrate those who made these Games count.For almost 12 days, the Indian gold rush had remained subdued. Then, just as the sun finally began showing up in Nagoya, the floodgates opened. Eleven gold medals came in the final two days, transforming what had threatened to become a disappointing campaign into a collection of stories about guts, resilience and glory.Dhanda, the 26-year-old from Sangatpura in Haryana, had set the tone by winning India’s first individual gold of these Games in the women’s trap event. The women went on to win 11 gold medals, apart from the three secured in mixed events.The contingent had 83 debutants, who accounted for 41 of India’s 85 medals — a clear indication of a changing guard across several sports.But if one athlete were to be picked as the face of that change, it would be difficult to look beyond 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod. The Maharashtra archer won two gold medals and a silver, but her biggest achievement went beyond the medal tally.She ended South Korea’s two-decade domination of the women’s recurve events by becoming the first Indian to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. It did not take her long to make the biggest stage of her young career her own.Even her Korean opponent Oh Ye-jin, whom Kumkum beat for the individual gold, was left impressed. “For a 17-year-old, she is very composed and has a very bright future,” Oh said.Another teenager, Prithika Pradeep, also emerged with two gold medals, adding to the sense that a new generation is beginning to announce itself. Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold.Behind every medal was a story of humble beginnings, survival in sport, societal pressures overcome and personal tragedies endured. That made the successes more than just entries in a medal table.They were not newcomers to the big stage. They had competed at the biggest of them all — the Olympics. But Nagoya offered unfinished business.Lovlina Borgohain had contemplated walking away from boxing after a difficult phase post the 2024 Paris Olympics. Instead, she returned to punch her way to gold.Parveen Hooda, returning after a doping ban, produced her own golden comeback. The bronze she had won in Hangzhou and subsequently lost became gold in Nagoya. Mirabai Chanu did not win gold, but her silver in the 49kg category had the weight of a champion’s achievement. It also completed her Asian Games medal collection.The women’s kabaddi team survived a tense battle against Iran. The women’s hockey team ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold. And Harmanpreet Kaur and her team ensured that cricket’s gold returned to India.Among the men, too, there were performances that demanded attention — Aman Sehrawat in wrestling, Ankush Panghal in boxing and Gulveer Singh in long-distance running among them.Yet, for all the celebration, there were glaring blanks. Manu Bhaker, one of India’s biggest sporting heroes, returned without a medal.There were plenty of nearmisses and some disastrous outings. India’s badminton return of a solitary bronze was another disappointment, particularly with a strong men’s doubles combination of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen in the squad.Table tennis also raised questions, while equestrian had its own share of run-ins between administrators and riders, alongside selectionrelated concerns but failed to add to the medal count.
Article Summary: India's final tally of 85 medals, including 21 gold, may represent a drop from the 106 medals and 28 golds won in Hangzhou. But numbers alone cannot tell the story of these Games. There were path-breakers everywhere, athletes who pushed through glass ceilings that had stood for years.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: PM Modi congratulates Team India, hails ‘determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit’
Article Text:
Indian contingent at the Asian Games closing ceremony and PM Narendra Modi

‘Immense joy to the nation’

Historic golds and landmark performances

Looking beyond Aichi-Nagoya

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday congratulated the Indian contingent for its performance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games , praising the athletes for representing the country with “determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit” as India concluded its campaign with 85 medals.India finished fourth on the medal table with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, ending the Games with its second-highest medal haul in Asian Games history. The tally was 21 medals fewer than the record 106 won at the Hangzhou edition in 2023.As the Games drew to a close in Nagoya on Sunday, Modi took to X to applaud the entire contingent and the medal winners while also expressing hope that the performances would help strengthen Indian sport at the grassroots level.In his post, the Prime Minister praised the athletes for their effort and sporting spirit throughout the continental showpiece.“As the Asian Games 2026 draw to a close, my compliments to every member of the Indian contingent for representing our nation with determination, passion and remarkable sporting spirit. Congratulations to all our medal winners, whose performances have brought immense joy to the nation.May these Games inspire even greater achievements in the years ahead. May they contribute to strengthening sports at the grassroots too,” Modi wrote.The Prime Minister’s message came after more than two weeks of competition involving athletes from 45 countries. The Aichi-Nagoya Games witnessed a string of record-breaking performances, including 54 world records.The Games formally concluded with a spectacular closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium in Nagoya on Sunday.India’s campaign was marked by several historic performances and successful title defences across disciplines.Both Indian cricket squads retained their Asian Games titles, while the men’s and women’s kabaddi sides also won gold. The men’s hockey side successfully defended its title with a 5-1 victory over Malaysia, while the women’s team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games gold by defeating China 1-0 in the final.There were also several breakthrough individual performances.Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games golf gold, while 17-year-old archer Kumkum Mohod created history by becoming the first Indian woman to win individual recurve gold at the continental showpiece.Mohod was also part of India’s historic women’s recurve team gold that ended South Korea’s seven-edition winning streak in the event. Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal, meanwhile, produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games to win the men’s 65kg freestyle gold.Boxer Lovlina Borgohain also joined an elite group of Indian women by becoming only the second after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games boxing gold.Athletics emerged as India’s biggest medal contributor with 24 medals, while shooting accounted for 15. Archery was the most successful sport in terms of gold medals, producing five top finishes.The campaign also provided a series of important milestones ahead of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with several young athletes making their mark on the continental stage.Earlier, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha named Mohod and Kalkal the inaugural recipients of the Jaspal Rana Award and Raja Randhir Singh Award respectively for the best female and male Indian sportspersons of the Games.With the Aichi-Nagoya campaign now complete, Modi’s message placed the emphasis not only on India’s medal tally but also on the broader legacy of the Games — inspiring another generation of athletes and strengthening the sporting ecosystem from the grassroots upwards.
Article Summary: India finished fourth on the medal table with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. The tally was 21 medals fewer than the record 106 won at the Hangzhou edition in 2023. Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the athletes for their effort and sporting spirit throughout the continental showpiece.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: PT Usha names Kumkum Mohod, Sujeet Kalkal as Team India’s MVPs after historic golds
Article Text:
Kumkum Mohod and Sujeet Kalkal

Mohod ends South Korea’s long reign

India's Kumkum Anil Mohod (Image: REUTERS)

Kalkal turns a lost final into gold

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sujeet Kalkal with coach after winning gold medal. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: Teenage archer Kumkum Mohod and wrestler Sujeet Kalkal have been recognised as the standout performers of India’s campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha naming them the inaugural recipients of the Jaspal Rana Award and Raja Randhir Singh Award respectively.The two awards have been instituted by the IOA to honour the best female and male sportspersons of the Games and commemorate the legacy of two stalwarts of Indian sport.Seventeen-year-old Mohod, making her Asian Games debut, won three medals, including two golds, while 23-year-old Kalkal produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games to claim gold in the men’s 65kg freestyle wrestling category.India finished fourth in the medal standings with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.Mohod was at the heart of one of the biggest breakthroughs for Indian archery in Aichi-Nagoya.Along with Ankita Bhakat and Kirti, she won the women’s recurve team gold, ending South Korea’s remarkable run of seven consecutive Asian Games titles in the event dating back to the 1998 Bangkok Games.Mohod then followed it with gold in the individual recurve event, ensuring that South Korea’s women failed to win a recurve gold at the Asian Games for the first time in the discipline’s history.Her individual triumph also secured a quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Usha praised Mohod’s ability to deliver under pressure and drew a parallel with the late Jaspal Rana, after whom the award has been named.“It is fitting that Kumkum is the first recipient of the Jaspal Rana Award, as Jaspal too burst onto the scene as a prodigy at the 1994 Asian Games. Her composure under pressure and her ability to find her best form when her back was to the wall augur extremely well for Indian Archery,” Usha said.The IOA president believes Mohod’s breakthrough could finally help Indian archery cross a long-standing barrier at the Olympics.“India's archers have been knocking on the door for more than a decade now, and I firmly believe that this performance by Kumkum and her recurve teammates has shattered the glass ceiling for Indian archery. India came close to winning a maiden Olympic medal in the sport at the Paris Olympics, and I am convinced that the final frontier will be breached at the Los Angeles Olympics,” Usha added.Kalkal, meanwhile, earned the Raja Randhir Singh Award after a gold-medal run that showcased his resilience and fighting spirit.The 23-year-old defeated reigning Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka of Japan in the semifinal before producing a stunning comeback against Abdulmazhid Kudiyev in the final.Kalkal trailed 2-9 with time running out but refused to give up, fighting back to win 10-9 in a dramatic finish. His triumph also continued India’s strong tradition in the 65kg category, following Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia, who won Asian Games gold in the same weight class in 2014 and 2018 respectively.Usha said it was Kalkal’s refusal to accept defeat that made his performance particularly special.“Wrestling is India's sport, and Sujeet's performance will be spoken of for years to come. The gold medal will be celebrated, but his never-say-die attitude and refusal to accept silver have earned him a special place in the hearts of all Indians,” she said.“Winning gold medals in elite competition is not easy, but equally important is the effort that goes in when your back is against the wall. I wish Sujeet all success in the years ahead and will be rooting for him to deliver India's first-ever wrestling gold medal at the Olympic Games in two years' time.”The IOA will felicitate Mohod and Kalkal at a ceremony in the coming days.Their selection provides a fitting individual recognition to two athletes whose performances stood out in India’s 85-medal campaign.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod and Sujeet Kalkal recognised as standout performers of India’s campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Teenage archer Mohod won three medals, including two golds, while 23-year-old KALKal produced one of the most dramatic comebacks of the Games. The two awards have been instituted by the IOA to honour the best female and male sportspersons.

Article Title: Asian Games: Leaner Indian contingent produces fewer golds but better return-per-medal - in numbers
Article Text:
Gold medallist India's players during the medal ceremony for the men's hockey event. (PTI Photo)

Where did the golds go?

Shooting, athletics behind the decline

Late surge takes India to 85 medals and fourth spot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The overall medal gap never disappeared

In late August, the Sports Ministry maintained that the qualification criteria for the Asian Games, put into place a year ago, would not change despite criticism. “The idea, from the very beginning, was to send a lean contingent. The criteria was announced a year ago, and everyone had the time to figure it out and qualify,” a Sports Ministry source told TimesofIndia.com back then. It was made clear that the objective was to have a contingent with only realistic medal contenders making the trip to Aichi-Nagoya."Let’s take an example. If somebody has to run inside 10 seconds to be a contender for a medal in the 100m event, should we send an athlete who clocks 15 seconds? We have set the criteria that if an athlete is in the top six in Asia, we will select him or her, otherwise not. We have followed that,” the source had said.The tennis squad went from 12 to 7. Several judokas and wushu athletes were removed from the initial list. From 44 players in 2022, no footballers were sent this time. There was also no place for 20 hoopers and 16 handball players.India had sent a 661-athlete contingent to the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Three years later, the final contingent that travelled to Japan was trimmed to 495 athletes.After 14 days of competition, India accounted for 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes for a combined 85 medals. For comparison, India had won 106 medals in China (28 golds, 38 silvers, and 40 bronze).As the contingent size dropped by 25.1%, the golds fell by nearly the same number (25%) and medals by 19.8%. India won 16 medals for every 100 athletes in Hangzhou. In Aichi-Nagoya, that figure rose to 17.2% — an improvement of about 7.3%.Stripped to the bare bones, India won 0.172 medals per athlete in Nagoya, against 0.160 in Hangzhou. Golds per athlete were essentially unchanged at about 0.042. Crudely, it counts every athlete sent, including those who did not medal. At the same time, teams as big as cricket (30 athletes), hockey (40) and kabaddi (24) account for a single medal in a discipline.So while India did not match its record 106-medal haul, its smaller contingent produced a slightly better medal return per athlete.The more complicated part of the comparison comes when gold medals are brought into the mix.India's gold medal tally fell from 28 to 21, a 25% decline — exactly in line with the reduction in the size of the contingent. The gold-medal yield was therefore virtually unchanged: 4.24 golds per 100 athletes in Hangzhou and 4.24 in Aichi-Nagoya.That suggests the smaller contingent was not, by itself, the reason India's gold tally fell. Rather, the composition of the medal haul changed.India's 2022 golds came heavily from three sports: shooting (seven), athletics (six), and archery (five), which is 18 of 28 (64%). In Nagoya, archery again delivered five, but shooting produced three and athletics one. Boxing, which won no gold in Hangzhou, won three, and wrestling won two after none. Golf added a gold courtesy Pranavi Urs. Squash, which won two golds in 2022, won none, despite the expectations from Anahat Singh, though the overall count of five medals did not change.The team sports carried more of the load. Cricket, hockey and kabaddi won six of India's 21 golds, up from five of 28. India completed a double title finish in all three. In 2022, hockey had produced one gold and one bronze.Athletics' podium shifted down a step. In 2022, it returned six golds, 14 silvers and nine bronzes. Now, despite a massive 75-plus-member contingent, it produced one gold, nine silvers and 14 bronzes.Shooting (4) and athletics (5) were the biggest reasons behind the drop in gold medals. Squash (2), Badminton (1), Tennis (1) and Equestrian (1) all also witnessed a drop in the yellow metal. Tennis, in fact, didn't produce a medal at all - a first in 40 years.In Hangzhou, shooting and athletics were the two biggest contributors to India's gold medal tally, producing seven and six gold medals, respectively. Together, they accounted for 13 of India's 28 golds. In Aichi-Nagoya, that combined figure collapsed to four. Shooting contributed three golds, while athletics produced one. India therefore lost nine gold medals from these two sports alone.The sub-par show from the athletes was made murkier by the withdrawals of 100m hurdler Jyothi Yarraji and triple jumper Praveen Chithravel. Both national record holders had skipped the Indian Athletics Series Final in prelude to the Asian Games, citing knee stress and a calf muscle pull, respectively.When it came to the Asian Games, Yarraji pulled out of the women's 100m hurdles first-round heats after "feeling pain" during the warm-up under rainy conditions.Chithravel, meanwhile, attempted his first jump but could not complete it, exiting the competition area clutching his calf in apparent pain. He was later taken away in a wheelchair. Men's 400m hurdler Yashas P., too, pulled out after starting his Heat.Coming to the shooters.India's 2026 shooting tally of 15 medals (3 golds, 8 silvers and 4 bronzes) was a 32% drop in total medal tally when compared to 22 in the previous continental showpiece. The gold haul took a 57% hit. Broken further, seven were team medals, five individual and three in mixed team events.The gold medals came in one individual (Neeru Dhanda in women's trap) and two mixed team events (Neeru and Kynan Chenai in mixed trap and Suruchi Phogat and Kamaljeet in mixed 10m air pistol).If the final medal tally tells one story, the daily trajectory tells another. Through the first 12 days of competition, India had won 10 gold medals in Aichi-Nagoya. In Hangzhou, India had already accumulated 21 golds by the same point.Then came the late surge in Japan.India won 11 gold medals over the final two days of its 2026 campaign — six on Day 13 and five on Day 14. That means 52.4% of India's entire gold haul came in the final two days. The equivalent figure in Hangzhou was 25%: seven of India's 28 golds came during the final two days.India had 13 golds by Day 8 in Hangzhou. At the same stage in Aichi-Nagoya, it had four. By Day 11, the gap was still eight golds — 18 to 10.But the final stretch changed the picture dramatically. India collected 18 golds across Days 13 and 14 in the two editions combined, but the distribution was very different: seven in Hangzhou and 11 in Aichi-Nagoya.On October 2, the women's recurve team of Ankita Bhakat, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum Mohod picked a gold. As did boxer Lovlina Borgohain on her birthday. Parveen Hooda also joined the party alongside wrestler Sujeet Kalkal's remarkable comeback, boxer Ankush Panghal's drought-ending gold, and the women's hockey team's triumph over China to seal an LA 2028 spot.A day later, archer Kumkum Mohod, golfer Pranavi Urs, wrestler Aman Sehrawat, the men's cricket team, and the men's hockey team gave the country plenty to celebrate with golden flourishes.The same late surge was visible in the total medal count, but it was not enough to close the gap with Hangzhou.After the first day, India had five medals in Hangzhou and two in Aichi-Nagoya.By Day 4, the difference had grown to 10 medals.By Day 8, it was 16.By Day 11, Hangzhou's cumulative tally stood at 80 medals, compared with 60 in Aichi-Nagoya — a 20-medal gap.India narrowed that deficit slightly over the next two days, reaching 76 medals against Hangzhou's 94 after Day 13.But the final day added nine medals in Aichi-Nagoya and 12 in Hangzhou, leaving the final difference to 21.
Article Summary: India had sent a 661-athlete contingent to the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Three years later, the final contingent that travelled to Japan was trimmed to 495 athletes. India accounted for 21 golds, 27 silvers and 37 bronzes for a combined 85 medals. For comparison, India had won 106 medals in China.

Article Title: ‘Learn from these Games and keep moving forward’: Abhinav Bindra’s message to Team India as LA Olympics beckons
Article Text:
Indian athletes leave the arena following the closing ceremony for the Asian Games in Nagoya. (AP Photo)

'Enormous respect to our athletes'

'LA is less than two years away'

NEW DELHI: Olympic gold medallist Abhinav Bindra has urged Indian athletes to learn from both the successes and disappointments of the Asian Games 2026, calling for stronger high-performance systems and a renewed focus on preparations for the Los Angeles Olympics, which are less than two years away.Congratulating India's athletes and support teams after the country finished fourth in the Aichi-Nagoya Games with 85 medals, Bindra highlighted the years of hard work and sacrifices behind their performances while stressing the need for an honest assessment of the campaign.India finished with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals, falling short of its record haul of 106 medals at Hangzhou 2023. However, the campaign produced several historic achievements, including gold-medal sweeps in men's and women's cricket, kabaddi and hockey.In a lengthy post on X on Sunday, Bindra thanked athletes, their families, coaches and support staff for their contributions before urging the sporting establishment to turn the lessons from Aichi-Nagoya into meaningful improvements."Congratulations to every Indian athlete and to Team India on the Asian Games. A Games campaign is never just the few days we see on television. It is years of early mornings, injuries, doubts, missed occasions and countless hours of work," Bindra wrote."So first and foremost, enormous respect to our athletes and also to their families who live this journey with them and make sacrifices that are rarely seen. To the coaches, support staff, federations, SAI, the Government and everyone working behind the scenes, THANK YOU!"The 2008 Beijing Olympics gold medallist in shooting acknowledged the breakthrough performances in Aichi-Nagoya, particularly those of young athletes who announced themselves on the continental stage. However, he stressed that disappointments must also be examined rather than simply forgotten."There have been some terrific breakthrough performances at these Games. Young athletes have announced themselves, others have stepped up to a new level, and there have been moments that give us a lot to be excited about. There have also been disappointments. That is sport, and every Games will have them. What matters now is how honestly we learn from them," he added.Bindra called for a more comprehensive approach to athlete development, arguing that high-performance programmes must provide the right expertise throughout an athlete's career rather than stepping in only when medals are within reach."High performance cannot only be about reacting when an athlete is close to a medal. We have to keep building systems that understand the athlete over several years," he wrote.He emphasised the importance of sports science, data-driven decisions, coaching, competition planning, training-load management, recovery and injury prevention, alongside building physical and mental resilience."Most importantly, the right expertise has to reach the athlete at the right stage of their career, not when it is already too late," he said.With the next Summer Olympics approaching, Bindra warned that the preparation window was shrinking and called for immediate action."LA is less than two years away. In Olympic sport, that is not a long time. The athletes who will stand on the podium there are already deep into their preparation today."His message was to celebrate the achievements, acknowledge shortcomings and return to work with renewed determination."Be proud of what has been achieved. Learn from these Games and keep moving forward. Wishing Team India everything good on the road to LA," he concluded.

Article Title: Asian Games: Olympic Council of Asia cites 54 world records to declare Aichi-Nagoya Games a success despite chaos
Article Text:
Ri Song Gum of North Korea had a sweep of world records at 49kg on 94-121-215. (AP Photo)

President of the OCA, Sheikh Joaan Bin Hamad Al Thani, left, looks at the Olympic Council of Asia flag as Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, PM of Qatar holds it. (AP Photo)

OCA highlights records, revenue growth

Logistical problems remain a concern

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) has defended the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games as a success, pointing to 54 world records, strong viewership and a nearly 20% increase in revenue despite persistent logistical problems that marred the continental sporting showpiece.OCA Director General Husain Al-Musallam said the record-breaking performances demonstrated that athletes had the environment needed to deliver exceptional results during the Games, which concluded on Sunday.A total of 54 world records, 11 junior world records and 89 continental records were set during the competition, providing the OCA with evidence of the event's sporting success despite complaints over accommodation and transportation."This achievement does not come without the best environment," Al-Musallam told reporters at a press conference on the final day of the Games."The athletes cannot perform if they don't have transportation. The athletes cannot perform if they don't have good healthcare. The athletes cannot perform if they don't eat food. Number talks, it's evidence. We are here to present you with the evidence."Al-Musallam also highlighted the financial sustainability of the Aichi-Nagoya model, arguing that major sporting events did not necessarily require expensive infrastructure projects that could become underused after the competition."We are happy to see that there is no big financial burden in the organising committee, and there is no white elephant staying in Nagoya or any place," he said.The OCA attributed the nearly 20% revenue increase compared with the Hangzhou 2023 Asian Games largely to digital growth and stronger viewership. India's hockey and cricket matches against Pakistan were among the fixtures that attracted large television audiences.Weightlifting was a major contributor to the record-breaking spectacle, with 25 senior world records established in the sport. North Korea led the way with 15 world records, while China also produced a series of outstanding performances.The Games attracted around 17,000 athletes and officials following a surge in late entries, approximately 2,000 more than initially projected.The sporting achievements, however, came against a backdrop of organisational difficulties. Without a dedicated athletes' village, participants were accommodated in hotels, container-style living units and a cruise ship.The unexpected increase in registrations strained accommodation and transport arrangements, prompting complaints about cramped rooms, small beds and unreliable transportation. Organising committee secretary general Satoshi Murate apologised for the problems.OCA officials nevertheless argued that the Games demonstrated the power of sport to bring countries together amid international tensions."When you look to the news, conflict everywhere - in Asia, outside Asia," Al-Musallam said. "Economic problems everywhere. But look at Asia, how united we are in sport."Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Games Coordination Committee, acknowledged that improvements were necessary."There is no Games without challenges. There are no Games without initial interruptions," Ikram said."In the future, we would like to see more sustainable solutions, more improvement and innovation ... but without compromising on the athletes' conditions."As Doha prepares to host the 2030 Asian Games, the Aichi-Nagoya edition has left organisers with two contrasting legacies: a remarkable collection of sporting records and a reminder that operational efficiency must match athletic ambition.
Article Summary: OCA defends Aichi-Nagoya 2026 as a success despite logistical problems. 54 world records, 11 junior world records and 89 continental records set during competition. North Korea led the way with 15 world records while China also produced a series of outstanding performances.

Article Title: Head coach Zinedine Zidane celebrates first home win as France crush Belgium 4-1 at Nations League

France scored four times in the final 14 minutes to beat Belgium 4-1 in the Nations League on Monday, giving Zinedine Zidane his first home victory as national coach.Belgium looked on course for a surprise win after Dodi Lukébakio put them ahead in the 35th minute. But France’s substitutes changed the game late on, with Désiré Doué, Rayan Cherki and Michael Olise scoring four goals between the 77th and 91st minutes.Doué levelled with a low shot in the 77th minute before Cherki’s effort took a strange deflection off Belgium goalkeeper Maarten Vandevoordt to put France ahead.Olise then scored twice in three minutes to complete a remarkable comeback.“Tonight, this is soccer, this is what we love,” Zidane said. “We faced some difficulties in the first half but that’s part of the game; it’s the kind of match you get from time to time. It’s good to set things right — which is what we did — and we managed to play an extraordinary second half.”Zidane praised his substitutes and the overall team effort.“We knew the substitutes could change the game because they are high-quality players,” Zidane said. “But, once again, it was a complete team performance; while the substitutes might have made the difference when they came on, everyone has been good over these past two weeks — everyone played their part, and that’s what stands out to me.”The result kept France top of Group A1, three points ahead of Italy, who beat Turkey 3-1. Belgium are third, four points behind France.“It’s a collective effort, too,” Olise said. "He (Zidane) brings in ideas, we follow them — we’ve done that well over the last four matches, we’re going to continue like this."Italy recovered from Turkey’s equaliser to win 3-1, with Gianluca Scamacca, Riccardo Calafiori and Pio Esposito scoring.Meanwhile, Victor Gyökeres scored again as Sweden beat Romania 1-0. Lionel Messi is about to play the final Argentina match of his career, but the farewell was reportedly not something he immediately welcomed. The occasion was always going to carry enormous significance after more than two decades with the national team, yet there was another issue behind the scenes, with Messi said to have questioned whether the match was really about saying goodbye or simply about making money from his name.Messi will play his 208th and final senior international for Argentina against Benin at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires on Tuesday, October 6, with the match beginning at 4:30 AM IST on Wednesday for viewers in India.The 39-year-old decided to end his Argentina career after the team's 2026 World Cup final defeat by Spain in New Jersey, where Messi left the pitch in tears after failing to make the influence he had hoped for in the match.His decision came during an already difficult period following his father's illness and subsequent death, with Messi acknowledging that ending his international career was a painful choice after everything he had given to Argentina.“I swear to you that I always gave it my all – not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football,” Messi said when announcing his retirement.According to Gazzetta dello Sport , however, Messi was initially reluctant to accept the idea of a farewell friendly against Benin because he believed the Argentine Football Association could be using the occasion to generate substantial revenue from his legacy.“Messi himself was not keen on the idea of this tribute match, as he viewed it as a final money-making venture by the AFA, using his name to secure millions in revenue,”reportedThe report also noted that Argentina head coach Lionel Scaloni had voiced some scepticism about the farewell, suggesting that he too had doubts over how the occasion was being put together.Messi ultimately agreed to play, although the match has continued to attract controversy around the way the fixture came together.Argentina's extended international break included three planned home friendlies against Bolivia, Burkina Faso and Benin, with the latter agreeing to become Messi's farewell opponent.“Benin has agreed to participate for free in Messi's farewell, content with merely appearing in a historic photograph.”The outlet also claimed that Benin's usual asking price would have been significant, while the AFA had tasked a Colombian agency with finding friendly opponents who would not demand a fee.The circumstances have added an unusual business element to what should otherwise be one of the most emotional nights in Argentine football, particularly with around 85,000 spectators expected at the Monumental.Members of Argentina's 2022 World Cup-winning squad and their families will attend the farewell, joining Messi alongside members of the country's emerging generation as the national team begins life beyond its longest-serving modern captain.Lionel Scaloni, who built the Argentina side around Messi and helped deliver the country's biggest successes, will also oversee a farewell for 38-year-old vice-captain Nicolás Otamendi.Rodrigo De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso were also called up specifically for the Benin match, raising the possibility that the game could become their final Argentina appearances as well.Messi's departure will close an international career that already places him among the most decorated players in Argentina's history, with a World Cup, two Copa America titles and the Finalissima among his major honours.He currently holds Argentina's records for appearances, goals and assists, having entered the farewell with 207 senior caps, 125 goals and 68 assists.His 125 goals leave him 69 ahead of Gabriel Batistuta, Argentina's second-highest goalscorer, while his 207 appearances leave him 61 ahead of Javier Mascherano.Messi will also leave Argentina as one of only four players to have made more than 200 senior international appearances, although Luka Modrić is expected to overtake him on the all-time list.Unlike Modrić and Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi leaves with a World Cup title alongside two Copa America victories, while Ronaldo's Portugal have won one European Championship during his international career.Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although he has acknowledged that his playing career could end sooner than expected following his father's death two months ago.Whatever happens after Tuesday night, Argentina's final match with Messi as captain will bring together the players who helped him finally win everything with the national team and the next generation preparing to take his place. For all the emotion surrounding the farewell, the reported hesitation from Messi shows that even his final night in the famous blue and white shirt was not quite as simple as it first appeared.

The 39-year-old announced his retirement after Argentina's 2026 World Cup final defeat by Spain in New Jersey. Article Title: 14-0! India U17 women crush Iraq for biggest-ever win in Asian Cup qualifiers; Anushka hits five

NEW DELHI: India’s U17 women’s side made a stunning start to their AFC U17 Women’s Asian Cup Qualifiers campaign, registering their biggest-ever victory with a 14-0 demolition of Iraq at the MP Selayang Stadium in Selayang, Malaysia, on Monday.The Young Tigresses broke their previous record wins of 12-0 against the UAE in 2014 and Sri Lanka in 2018 with a ruthless attacking display that left Iraq struggling to cope for much of the contest.Anushka Kumari led the rout with five goals and was named Player of the Match, while skipper and centre-back Abhista Basnett scored twice. Silky Devi Sorokhaibam, Thandamoni Baskey, Nira Chanu Longjam, Pritika Barman, Joya and Alva Devi Senjam were also on the scoresheet.India dominated from the opening whistle, combining ceaseless running, close marking and sharp one-touch passing to deny Iraq time and space.Joakim Alexandersson’s midfield controlled the game with neat distribution and compact positioning, while Redima Devi Chingkhamayum, Thandamoni, Silky and Alva repeatedly used the width to stretch the Iraqi defence.The pressure soon told as India raced into a commanding lead.Anushka struck twice before Silky scored twice for her first international goals. Thandamoni and Nira added one each as India went into the interval with a remarkable 7-0 lead.Anushka completed her fourth goal just two minutes after the restart, sweeping home a cross from Alva. Substitute Pritika then made it 9-0 by converting a rebound after substitute goalkeeper Asmaa Shivan Ahmed had initially denied India.The floodgates remained open, although the Iraqi goalkeeper produced a couple of good saves to prevent the margin from growing further.Then came an unexpected interruption.Play was halted after 64 minutes because of inclement weather, with lightning and thunder forcing the players off the field. The match resumed after a 30-minute stoppage.The weather break did little to slow India down.Abhista rose highest to head home Ritu Badaik’s dipping corner from the right before Anushka added her fifth, placing the ball into the net from just outside the box.Joya then found an empty net after Pritika rounded the goalkeeper and squared the ball across the box, taking India to 12-0 and level with their previous record victory.Abhista headed in another Ritu corner to make it 13-0 and set a new benchmark for India at this age-group level.The record was extended further in added time. Yashica Haribabu’s free-kick came back off the bar before Abhista’s follow-up effort dropped into the six-yard box, allowing Alva to head home and complete the 14-0 rout.India will next face Syria on October 8 at 1pm IST before taking on hosts Malaysia on October 11 at 6:30pm IST in Group E. Only the group winners will qualify for the AFC U17 Women’s Asian Cup China 2027.
